section_summary: This section (pages 1-69) of State Department file 894.00 covers U.S. government intelligence, internal memoranda, diplomatic despatches, and military reports from September 1942 through March 1943 concerning internal political, economic, and social developments in wartime Japan. Key topics include evaluations of General Hideki Tojo's cabinet, the resignation of Foreign Minister Shigenori Togo, the creation of the Greater East Asia Ministry, and potential friction between Japan and the Soviet Union. The documents also feature in-depth firsthand reports on civilian living conditions, food rationing, morale, and shipping vulnerabilities in Japan obtained from repatriated YMCA secretary Russell L. Durgin and Argentine diplomat Ramon Lavalle, as well as analyses of the totalitarian restructuring under the Imperial Rule Assistance Association (Taisei Yokusankai) and structural weaknesses within Japanese society.

subfiles.about: Elbridge Durbrow briefs Soviet Counselor Andrei Gromyko on contrasting Chinese and neutral European interpretations regarding the resignation of Japanese Foreign Minister Togo and Japanese policy toward the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: State Department official Elbridge Durbrow records a meeting held at Ray Atherton's suggestion with Andrei A. Gromyko, Counselor of the Soviet Embassy. Durbrow informed Gromyko of a September 5 telegram from Chungking in which a Chinese Foreign Office official interpreted Premier Hideki Tojo's assumption of the foreign minister portfolio as an indication that Japanese-Soviet diplomatic relations had failed and military action was being prepared. In contrast, Durbrow shared neutral European reports indicating that Togo's resignation stemmed from internal opposition to the creation of the Greater East Asia Ministry. An attached September 8 memorandum summarizes these two divergent assessments.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation on Chinese and Neutral Interpretations of Togo's Resignation and Japanese-Soviet Relations

subfiles.about: Stanley K. Hornbeck reports a telephone conversation with Captain McCrea regarding naval press conference disclosures of Chinese estimates predicting a Japanese attack on the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Political Adviser Stanley K. Hornbeck reports that Captain John L. McCrea, Naval Aide to the President, telephoned regarding statements made by the Secretary of the Navy at a press conference concerning Ambassador Gauss's telegram from Chungking. The telegram conveyed Chinese estimates that Japan planned to attack the Soviet Union if Japanese demands were not favorably answered following General Tojo's takeover of the Foreign Ministry. President Roosevelt had requested that Under Secretary Sumner Welles bring this matter to the attention of the Soviet Ambassador, and Hornbeck undertook to inform Secretary of State Cordell Hull. An attached September 8 memorandum provides the background summary of the Chinese and neutral reports.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Chinese Estimates of Japanese Intentions toward the Soviet Union

subfiles.about: William L. Langer transmits an OSS confidential interview report with Russell L. Durgin regarding living conditions, rationing, and morale in Tokyo following the outbreak of the Pacific War.
subfiles.summary: William L. Langer, Director of the Branch of Research and Analysis at the Office of Strategic Services, transmits to Assistant Secretary of State Breckinridge Long a copy of Interview No. 16, conducted in August 1942 aboard the exchange ship S.S. Gripsholm with Russell L. Durgin. Durgin, a longtime YMCA secretary in Tokyo who remained largely free to move about the city until mid-1942, describes the treatment of American nationals and missionaries, widespread food shortages, and the tonari gumi neighborhood rationing system. He details severe scarcities of rice, meat, milk, clothing, leather, gasoline, and metals, as well as police surveillance of Axis nationals and public attitudes toward the war.
subfiles.title: Transmittal of OSS Interview No. 16: Conditions in Tokyo after December 7, 1941

subfiles.about: Assistant Secretary of State Breckinridge Long acknowledges receipt of the OSS interview with Russell L. Durgin regarding conditions in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Assistant Secretary of State Breckinridge Long writes to Dr. William L. Langer, Director of the Branch of Research and Analysis at the Office of Strategic Services, acknowledging receipt of his letter of November 23, 1942. Long expresses appreciation for transmitting the report of the interview conducted with Russell L. Durgin following his repatriation from Tokyo on the S.S. Gripsholm.
subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Receipt of OSS Interview with Russell L. Durgin

subfiles.about: William L. Langer transmits a copy of OSS Interview No. 16 with Russell L. Durgin to George Gordon of the Division of Foreign Activity Correlation.
subfiles.summary: William L. Langer of the Office of Strategic Services transmits Copy No. 13 of Interview No. 16 to George Gordon, Acting Chief of the Division of Foreign Activity Correlation in the Department of State. The enclosed interview, conducted aboard the exchange ship S.S. Gripsholm in August 1942, details Russell L. Durgin's observations of wartime conditions in Tokyo. The report covers the status of American residents, strict rationing of staple foods and materials, public grumbling over scrap metal collections, surveillance of German and Italian residents, and Japanese attitudes regarding the war and the Emperor.
subfiles.title: Transmittal of OSS Interview No. 16: Conditions in Tokyo after December 7, 1941 (Copy No. 13)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing a Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on the newly created Japanese Ministry of Greater East Asiatic Affairs.
keywords: Ministry of Greater East Asiatic Affairs
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet indexes an underlying memorandum dated November 5, 1942, prepared by H. Merrell Benninghoff of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs and filed under decimal number 894.002/525. The original document transmits intelligence derived from Tokyo radio broadcasts regarding the establishment and organization of the new Japanese Ministry of Greater East Asiatic Affairs.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note regarding Japanese Ministry of Greater East Asiatic Affairs

subfiles.about: Ambassador Gauss reports unverified rumors from Chungking concerning an alleged assassination attempt on Premier Tojo and new Japanese wartime economic measures.
subfiles.summary: American Ambassador Clarence E. Gauss transmits unconfirmed intelligence obtained from unofficial sources in Chungking regarding domestic developments in Japan. Rumors indicate that the postponement of the Imperial Diet was caused by an unsuccessful assassination attempt on Premier Hideki Tojo rather than illness, and that Tojo received expanded powers from the Privy Council. Other unverified reports assert that forty percent of Japanese textile spindles will be scrapped for metal, chemical production will be increased, tobacco prices have been doubled for revenue, and the national budget has risen to twenty-five billion yen.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 116 from Chungking on Rumors of Tojo Assassination Attempt and Economic Measures

subfiles.about: J. Edgar Hoover transmits an FBI intelligence memorandum analyzing the social, political, moral, and spiritual outlook of the Japanese people and exile groups in Argentina.
subfiles.summary: FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover transmits to Assistant Secretary of State Adolf A. Berle, Jr., a confidential memorandum evaluating Japanese commercial, political, moral, and spiritual conditions. The memorandum describes the severe hardships faced by Japanese laborers and women, the lack of labor protections, and factional struggles within the military and political elite. It discusses moral conditions, including widespread licensed prostitution and geisha houses, as well as Emperor worship and religious traditions. Finally, it assesses the potential for Japanese expatriates in Argentina, disillusioned by traditional social structures, to organize an undercover opposition movement against the imperial government.
subfiles.title: FBI Memorandum on Japanese Outlook

subfiles.about: Stanley K. Hornbeck circulates an analytical study detailing fundamental industrial, psychological, social, and political vulnerabilities of Japan in total war.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck forwards an extensive analytical study dated April 30, 1942, entitled 'Elements of Weakness in the Japanese People and in the Japanese Position,' commending it as first-rate and noting a copy was provided to Joseph C. Grew. The monograph analyzes critical weaknesses in the Japanese war effort, emphasizing that American industrial capacity will inevitably outpace Japanese war production. It highlights profound social and political cleavages beneath the surface of wartime unity, citing a history of political assassinations, the February 26 Incident of 1936, and internal military rivalries. The study also identifies operational rigidities, poor public health and high mortality, deep-seated superstitions, suppression of women, and diplomatic isolation resulting from aggressive foreign policies.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Elements of Weakness in the Japanese People and in the Japanese Position

subfiles.about: Military Attaché report detailing the foundation, restructuring, rules, and leadership of the Taisei Yokusankai and Yokusan Seijikai in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Lieutenant Colonel Morris B. DePass, Jr., Acting Military Attaché in Chungking, transmits an intelligence report based on official regulations translated by Free French agents regarding the Taisei Yokusankai (Imperial Rule Assistance Association). The report traces the origins of the movement founded under Premier Fumimaro Konoye in 1940 and its reorganization under Premier Hideki Tojo and the Yokusan Seijikai (Imperial Rule Assistance Political Society) in 1942 to achieve total political and economic mobilization. It describes the functions of the Central Co-operative Council, outlines the responsibilities of key bureaus, and provides a roster of principal officers including Tojo, Kisaburo Ando, and Fumio Goto. Complete translations of the sixteen governing articles regulating headquarters and local branch structures are appended.
subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report No. 1151: Organization of Japanese National Association of Political Service (Taisei Yokusankai)
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division, War Department General Staff

subfiles.about: Consular despatch transmitting detailed debriefings of Argentine diplomat Ramon Lavalle on internal conditions, morale, shipping losses, and foreign nationals in wartime Japan.
subfiles.summary: American Consul Burton Y. Berry in Istanbul forwards a report based on extensive interviews conducted by Vice Consul Roy M. Melbourne with Ramon Lavalle, former Argentine Consul in Hong Kong and Special Attaché in Tokyo. Lavalle recounts an alleged poisoning attempt against him in Tokyo and assesses Japanese civilian morale as solid, though apprehensive over Soviet military strength. He describes worsening food shortages, strict economic controls, an acute commercial shipping crisis that shipping executives believe will cost Japan the war, and a November 1942 disaster in Yokohama harbor where explosions destroyed six vessels including German raiders. The despatch also details the removal of German Ambassador Eugen Ott after a dispute with the Gestapo, harsh surveillance of American nisei, the arrest of university professors, and Lavalle's subsequent journey across Siberia to Turkey.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 847: A Report on Current Conditions in Japan

subfiles.about: Division of Current Information memorandum reviewing the referral to OWI of Mr. Heller's psychological warfare proposal and noting departmental misgivings.
subfiles.summary: An official in the Division of Current Information records the procedural history of a proposal submitted by Mr. Heller in February 1943. Although the suggestion was initially shared with the Office of War Information (OWI) on February 15 following Far Eastern Affairs concurrence, subsequent reservations voiced by Stanley K. Hornbeck led the Department to clarify to OWI that the idea did not have official endorsement. The author notes that the carbon copy of the reply to Heller is missing from the file and urges that an answer or acknowledgment be dispatched immediately if not already done.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Departmental Handling of Heller Psychological Warfare Proposal

subfiles.about: Max W. Bishop recommends transmitting Mr. Heller's suggestion on psychological warfare to the Office of War Information.
subfiles.summary: Max W. Bishop of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs writes to John K. Caldwell concerning an incoming letter dated February 2, 1943 from Mr. Heller, which had been referred to the division by Joseph C. Grew. Bishop expresses the view that Heller's suggestion merits consideration by an agency such as the Office of War Information (OWI). He proposes that if Caldwell concurs, a copy of the communication should be forwarded to OWI.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Referral of Heller Letter to the Office of War Information

subfiles.about: Joseph C. Grew refers an incoming letter from Mr. Heller to the Division of Far Eastern Affairs for appropriate reply.
subfiles.summary: Former Ambassador Joseph C. Grew, serving as Special Assistant to the Secretary of State, forwards a letter from Mr. Heller dated February 2, 1943 to the Division of Far Eastern Affairs. The referral memorandum directs the division to draft an appropriate departmental reply to the correspondent.
subfiles.title: Referral Memorandum for Letter from Mr. Heller
